title: A Radiators for the Wardrobe
premise: Gideon Crane, night librarian in a city that never quite sleeps, has spent years cataloguing silences—especially those of their late mother, whose funeral draws a stranger who calls the family by an old, buried surname. The stranger, Vera, carries a letter containing one untranslatable sentence in their grandmother's hand, and the house where Gideon grew up goes to auction in nine days. As Gideon and Vera decode the sentence together, loyalty to the family's chosen story collides with the truth of why they were renamed and hidden. In the end, Gideon reads the translated sentence aloud at the house sale—not to stop it, but to let the past be sold honestly—and chooses Vera, and visibility, over the safety of being unsaid.
about_author: Petra Sterling is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing other people's unfinished letters before turning to fiction. They write at night, in libraries, about the things families keep in inventory but never shelve.

chapters.title: The Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. At their mother's sparsely attended funeral, Gideon performs their usual role: invisible keeper of records, reciting the eulogy from index cards. A stranger named Vera appears, addresses the mourners by the family's abandoned surname, 'Halloway,' and leaves without explanation. The emotional beat is quiet rupture—the first crack in a life built on careful silence—and Gideon's compulsion to catalogue begins to fail them.

chapters.title: A Letter in the Grandmother's Hand
chapters.summary: Alternating POV between Gideon and Vera. Vera returns to the library at 3 a.m. with a water-stained letter written by the grandmother Gideon never knew existed, containing a single sentence in a dying dialect no translator will touch. Vera reveals she was promised answers by Gideon's mother years ago. The beat is wary alliance: two people who both loved a woman who lied beautifully, circling the same locked room.

chapters.title: Nine Days to Closing
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV, with interludes of the letter itself. As the house sale deadline looms, Gideon uncovers why the family was renamed—a scandal, a protection, a betrayal involving Vera's own kin—and confronts their brother, who begs them to let the auction bury everything. Torn between loyalty and truth, Gideon nearly burns the letter. The emotional beat is rising dread: every answer costs a relationship, and the sentence is almost legible.

chapters.title: Read Aloud Before the Sale
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV, closing with Vera's. On auction day, Gideon stands in the empty childhood house and translates the sentence at last—it is an apology and an instruction: remember us by our real name, or not at all. They read it aloud to the assembled buyers, then sign the papers anyway, letting the house go but keeping the name. The final beat is resolution as choice: Gideon steps out into daylight beside Vera, visible, said, and staying.
